title: The ark opens
hookLine: the congregation stands as the Torah is carried around and greeted with a kiss

lines: A PARADE IN A SMALL SPACE.
cards: On Monday and Thursday mornings, on Shabbat, festivals and the new month, the service reaches a moment like a parade in a very small space. Someone pulls back a curtain at the front of the room. The doors behind it open.
Everyone stands. A scroll in a velvet cover, or a carved wooden case, is lifted out and carried through the aisles. People reach out as it passes.
A woman touches it with the corner of her prayer book. A child is lifted up to kiss it.

teach.b: Why those days? The Talmud, in Bava Kamma 82a, starts with a verse: in the wilderness, the people walked three days and found no water.
The rabbis read water as Torah, and say the prophets of that generation made sure the people would never again go three days without it: so, a reading on Shabbat, on Monday and on Thursday.
Later, the Talmud says, Ezra the scribe added to the system. As the ark opens, many congregations sing a verse Moses said when the ark set out in the wilderness.
In the old Jewish translation: "Rise up, O LORD, and let Thine enemies be scattered." Then a line from Isaiah: "for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem."
The cabinet shares its name with that traveling ark: Ashkenazim call it the aron kodesh, the holy ark, and Sephardim often call it the heichal, the palace. The congregation stands while it's open.
The Talmud, in Kiddushin, argues: if people rise for those who study the Torah, how much more for the Torah itself.
Then the scroll is carried around. People don't usually touch the parchment; they touch the cover with the fringes of their tallit or the edge of a prayer book, and kiss that.

In many Sephardi communities, the scroll lives in a hard case and stands upright to be read. The scroll the whole room stood for isn't locked away or kept on a stage. It's brought down the aisles, close enough to touch.

how: On Monday and Thursday mornings, Shabbat, festivals, Rosh Chodesh and fast days, the ark is opened and the congregation stands; the Torah is carried around the synagogue, and people touch its cover with a tallit fringe or prayer book and kiss it.

games.why: Bava Kamma 82a credits the prophets of that generation with readings on Shabbat, Monday and Thursday; Ezra added to them later.

practice: Somewhere in your home is one thing that carries more than its weight: a grandparent's book, a photo, a letter, a ring, a child's first drawing.

Stand in front of it if you can, or stand where you are and picture it, still for a moment, the way you'd stand for someone who walked into the room. If you like, touch it gently, the way people touch the scroll.

wordCard.voice: Aron kodesh. The holy ark: the cabinet whose doors open for the Torah, when the congregation stands and the scroll is carried through the room and kissed.
